name: Aisha Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a drylining carpenter for Meridian Interiors, and right now we're on the new wing at St Luke's hospital. I build the inside walls and ceilings, the metal stud frames, then the plasterboard, and all the fire-stopping around pipes so fire can't spread between rooms. I start the day with my tablet, checking the 3D model of the building against what's actually there. I love it when a corridor lines up perfectly with the drawing. The boards are heavy, though, and my knees have started telling me about every one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You start with a tablet and a 3D model. How much tech is in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot, for someone my age. I use an AI app on the tablet every day to check if a wall clashes with a pipe or a duct before I build it, and the young ones come to me to ask how. My husband Jonas drove buses until his diabetes made him stop, so he's on a small early pension. Two years ago we paid off our son Karim's debts when his café failed, so now we've got maybe three weeks of money. There are only three interiors firms in this region, all chasing the same hospital and school contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, I was looking forward to robots carrying the boards. At work I'd shrug and get on. Online I'd probably share something about how the clash-checking apps are still the best bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes, and that's okay but not great. The money's still low, the boards are still heavy, and I've still got about eight years to go on bad knees. AI was going to help with the heavy part, and in this picture it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep using the apps I've got. I'd ask Meridian to put me forward as a supervisor on the next hospital job, since I already do half the checking. And I'd start putting fifty a month back into savings now Karim's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like the bus came and it was the old one again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you already do half the checking. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the St Luke's job I found a clash between a fire damper and a ceiling grid two weeks before we built it. The app flagged it, I checked it on site, and we saved maybe three days of ripping out. The site manager said thanks, but I'm still paid as an ordinary carpenter. That's the part that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a supervisor job mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more money, maybe a hundred a week, and less lifting. That's the difference between Jonas and me getting a week away once a year or not. It'd also mean my knees last until pension age.

S0.say: That's a shame, I was looking forward to robots carrying the boards. The clash-checking apps are still the best bit.
S0.think: Nothing changes, which is okay but not great, with low pay, heavy boards and eight years to go on bad knees. AI was going to help with the heavy part, and here it doesn't.
S0.do: Keeps working and using her apps, and asks Meridian to put her forward as a supervisor since she already does much of the checking. Starts saving fifty a month now her son's debts are paid.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like the old bus turning up again.
S0.quote: Like the bus came and it was the old one again.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is mildly disappointed that AI didn't take the heavy lifting, which she'd welcome. She already does checking work above her pay grade and wants to be recognised for it. Her thin savings come from rescuing her son, not from low spending discipline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be the people who know how to use it. At work I'd offer to show anyone the apps. Online I'd post the occasional before-and-after of what the tools caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. The jobs that grow are the ones that check, plan and set out walls with machines, and I'm already doing that. The risk is that Meridian brings in a 25-year-old with a degree instead of promoting me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book myself on a setting-out course this winter, where you use a laser station to mark exactly where every wall goes, about six hundred, and I'd pay it in instalments if Meridian won't. I'd go to the manager with a list of every clash I've caught this year and ask for the digital coordinator role. And I'd learn whatever robot layout tools come in first, before anyone asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even hopeful. For once, being the one who likes gadgets is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six hundred in instalments on three weeks of savings. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hundred a month for six months, and I'd stop buying lunch on site, that's the hundred right there. Jonas would grumble about packed lunches for him too. But if it gets me the coordinator job, it pays back in two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You worried about a young graduate getting the job. What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be annoyed for about a day. Then I'd teach them, because they'd need it, and make sure everyone saw who knew more. In my experience, the site always ends up asking the person who's actually built the thing.

S1.say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be the people who know how to use it. I'd show anyone the apps and post what the tools caught.
S1.think: This is good for me, because the growing jobs check, plan and set out walls with machines, which I already do. The risk is Meridian hiring a young graduate instead of promoting me.
S1.do: Books a setting-out course this winter for about six hundred, paid in instalments by giving up bought lunches. Takes a list of caught clashes to her manager to ask for the digital coordinator role, and learns robot layout tools before anyone asks.
S1.feel: Calm and even hopeful, because liking gadgets is finally worth something.
S1.quote: For once, being the one who likes gadgets is worth something.
S1.fieldNote: This picture plays to her strengths and she knows it. Her worry is about being passed over, not replaced, and she has a practical answer even for that. She pays for her own training rather than expecting a union or government to, which fits her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should help people through it, but I'd also say we can't stop it. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the robots now. Online I'd keep my head down, it'd be a shouting match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried but not hopeless. I'd be 60, and if robots can build walls, someone still needs to set them up and check them, and I could be that someone. But there won't be many of those jobs, and three weeks of savings doesn't buy much time if I guess wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to whichever firm brings the robots in first and ask to be on that crew, even if it means leaving Meridian. If the robot jobs are in the big city two hours away, Jonas and I would rent somewhere smaller there, we've talked about it before. I'd cut everything, sell my car and use the train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy anxious, though, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those two years before it arrives look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend them getting known as the robot person. Every trial, every demo day at the supplier, I'd be there with my tablet. I'd ask the robot company's engineers stupid questions until they weren't stupid any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move with Jonas. How would he take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be fine, honestly, he's retired and he likes cities more than me. The harder part is our grandkids, Karim's two, who live ten minutes away now. We'd be the grandparents who visit on Sundays instead of doing school pick-ups, and I'd miss that.

S2.say: It's too fast and the government should help people through, but we can't stop it. I'd tell everyone at work to learn the robots now.
S2.think: I'd be worried but not hopeless, because someone still has to set up and check the robots. But those jobs will be few, and three weeks of savings doesn't buy time if I guess wrong.
S2.do: Spends the two years getting known as the robot person at every trial and demo. Asks to join the first robot crew even if it means leaving Meridian, plans to move with Jonas to a smaller rental in the city, and sells her car.
S2.feel: Anxious, but busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: I'd ask the robot company's engineers stupid questions until they weren't stupid any more.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture she stays anxious rather than alarmed, because she can see a concrete role for herself and has the skills to chase it. Thin savings are her main risk. The cost she feels most is giving up daily time with her grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, so people should use it. At work I'd say the same as before, learn it now. Online I'd post a few tips, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better for me. I'd get the setting-out course done, get a couple of robot trials under my belt, and be the obvious person when it arrives. And at 63 I'd only need a few years in that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the setting-out course in the first year and ask Meridian to put me on every trial. I'd save the extra if I get the coordinator job, maybe a hundred a week, so we have something by the time it lands. I wouldn't need to move straight away, I'd see where the work ends up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. More planning than worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save a hundred a week if you got the job. What would you be saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cushion, mostly, so if I'm wrong about the robot jobs we don't fall straight off a cliff. And maybe to help Karim again if he needs it, though he's promised he won't. Five years of a hundred a week would be more savings than we've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, who's 50 and the best board hanger I know, but he won't touch the tablet. He thinks it's a fad. I'd keep nudging him, but you can't make someone learn.

S3.say: Five years is a fair run-up, so people should use it. I'd keep telling people at work to learn it now.
S3.think: I'd get the course and some robot trials done and be the obvious person when it arrives. At 63 I'd only need a few years in that job.
S3.do: Does the setting-out course in the first year and joins every Meridian trial. Saves about a hundred a week if promoted, as a cushion in case she's wrong, and holds off on moving until she sees where the work goes.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, more planning than worrying.
S3.quote: Five years of a hundred a week would be more savings than we've ever had.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her build both skills and a cushion, and she sees the cushion as insurance against her own guess being wrong. She worries about colleagues who dismiss the tools. Her plans are personal and self-funded rather than collective.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone to get ready, so there's no excuse for not trying. At work I'd help the younger ones plan. I'd keep it mostly off social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd be retiring around the time it lands. With ten years I can move into checking and setting-out on my own schedule, save my knees, and finish well. It looks fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Meridian and do the setting-out course in the next year or two, then aim for the coordinator role. I'd save steadily, fifty a month now and more if I'm promoted. I'd keep learning each new tool as it comes, the way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This one feels like a slow river I can swim in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calm about this one. Is there anything that would make you lose sleep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pensions, maybe. If AGI means governments have less tax coming in, I don't know what happens to the state pension. I'd be relying on it completely, so yes, that's the one thing. But I can't do much about it from a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim's 33 and he's already failed once with the café, so he's scared of trying things. I'd tell him to learn the tools now, while it's slow, and to go into something where you deal with people. He'd listen to me more than his dad, he always has.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for anyone to get ready, so there's no excuse for not trying. I'd help the younger ones at work plan.
S4.think: At 68 I'd be retiring around when it lands. With ten years I can move into checking and setting-out on my own schedule and finish well.
S4.do: Keeps working at Meridian, does the setting-out course in the next year or two and aims for the coordinator role. Saves fifty a month and more if promoted, and keeps learning each new tool as it arrives.
S4.feel: Calm, like a slow river she can swim in.
S4.quote: This one feels like a slow river I can swim in.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she is calm, because her skills and her retirement timing both line up. Her only real worry is the state pension, which she depends on completely. She'd pass on her approach to her son, who is more risk-shy after his failed café.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though I'd still fight in it. The danger is that the few robot jobs go to young people with degrees, and people like me with thirty years on site get skipped. What would help is a proper fast course, paid while you train, for people who already know the building trade, so our experience counts for something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the knees and backs. People think robots on site are only bad news, but a robot lifting plasterboard would add years to my working life. The question isn't robots or no robots, it's who gets to run them.

headlineQuote: The question isn't robots or no robots, it's who gets to run them.
portrait: Aisha Weber is a 58-year-old drylining carpenter on a hospital extension, the person younger workers ask about the tablet and the AI clash-checking app she uses every day. She has three weeks of savings after paying off her son's café debts, a husband on an early pension and knees that feel every board. She stays calm in the Plateau and Steady Disruption, where she plans a setting-out course and a push for a coordinator role. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious but busy, ready to move cities for a robot crew, and with five or ten years she settles into planning and calm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the few robot jobs could go to young graduates and skip people with decades on site.
whatWouldHelp: A fast, paid course for experienced building workers so their site experience counts towards the new roles.
